content: The Mantoux test, also known as the tuberculin skin test (TST), PPD test, or TB skin test, is the standard method for determining whether an individual is infected with Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Proper administration and interpretation of the TST require adherence to standardized procedures, adequate training, supervision, and practice. To perform the test, 0.1 mL of tuberculin purified protein derivative (PPD) is injected intradermally into the inner surface of the forearm using a tuberculin syringe. The needle should be positioned with the bevel facing upward. When administered correctly, the injection creates a pale, raised area of skin (referred to as a wheal) measuring 6 to 10 mm in diameter. The reaction to the skin test must be evaluated between 48 and 72 hours after the injection. If the patient does not return within 72 hours, the test will need to be repeated. The reaction is assessed by measuring the diameter of the induration (a palpable, raised, hardened area or swelling) in millimeters. It is important to note that erythema (redness) should not be measured. The measurement of the induration should be taken across the forearm, perpendicular to its long axis. The interpretation of the tuberculin skin test depends on two key factors: 1. The size of the induration in millimeters. 2. The individual’s risk of being infected with tuberculosis and their likelihood of progressing to active disease if infected. The test is contraindicated only in individuals who have experienced severe reactions to a previous TST, such as necrosis, blistering, anaphylactic shock, or ulceration. It is not contraindicated for infants, children, pregnant women, individuals infected with HIV, or those who have received the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine. In some individuals infected with M. tuberculosis, the ability to react to tuberculin may diminish over time. When these individuals are tested years after the initial infection, they may exhibit a false-negative reaction. However, the TST can stimulate the immune system, potentially leading to a positive or boosted reaction upon subsequent testing. Administering a second TST after an initial negative reaction is referred to as two-step testing. Two-step testing is particularly useful for the initial skin testing of adults who will undergo periodic retesting, such as healthcare workers or residents of nursing homes. This approach helps reduce the likelihood of misinterpreting a boosted reaction to a subsequent TST as a recent infection.
